transcription.text: It's equipment review time again, and this week I've got a lab power supply. It's the
BK Precision 1697 switch mode DC laboratory power supply. Now, you may not have heard of BK
Precision before, but they make a fairly comprehensive range of a whole bunch of gear,
not just power supplies, but multimeters, oscilloscopes and electronic loads and all
sorts of stuff. And they're a Canadian company and they make some decent low to mid-range
test equipment. So let's check this one out. Now, this one is their bottom-of-the-range
programmable supply. It's 40 volts, 5 amps switch mode. It goes from 1 to 40 volts,
fully adjustable and fully programmable. You can hook it up to a PC and you can do some quite
fancy stuff with it. And it retails for about US$330, which is pretty good value for a programmable
bench supply. Now, the first thing you notice about this supply is its modern appearance.
So you have a large LCD display, entry keypad, and a single large, very nice jog shuttle
dial here. And it looks really funky. But when it comes to power supplies, I'm an old-fashioned
kind of guy. I like my voltage and current knobs and nice big independent readouts.
And of course, the first thing we're going to do is take it apart. Okay, we have the cover off. Now,
let's take a look inside, shall we? The cover came off fairly easily. And we have standard
single-sided PCB construction. Looks very typical of a sort of a good quality switch mode
power supply. I can see some temperature sensing down there on the heat sink. That's for over
temperature protection. And there's a vertical board here. I'm not sure what that does, but
it looks like probably some of the control circuitry. And yeah, it's not bad construction
at all. The fan is actually temperature controlled as well. So it will actually come on only when it
needs to, which is really handy. And yeah, I like it. Construction is quite nice. All right, the first
thing we're going to check out is the ripple and noise. It has a claimed ripple and noise of 25
millivolts. And if we take a look at the output here, we can see it's around 13 to 15 millivolts
peak-to-peak noise. And there's a little bit of ripple there, but it's not bad. It certainly
seems to meet its spec. And yep, that's fairly typical of a switch mode of this
design and this price range. Now one of the most important criteria in a lab bench supply is that
it doesn't overshoot when you switch the load on. So let's try that here. I've set up the
oscilloscope to trigger, the output's off, and I'll switch it on. Shift, output on, and bingo! We've
captured something, and there is some overshoot on here. Not too much. It seems to have clamped it
fairly well, but there seems to be a bit of a little bit of a ramp up there, which is nothing
too much to worry about. And then you can see it kicking in and regulating just nicely. So
I've certainly seen a hell of a lot worse than that. So that's pretty good.
Now there's another handy feature of this unit, in that you can actually set up a maximum output
voltage. So if you take your jog shuttle here, you can actually adjust the voltage of course.
There's the minimum, one volt. You can actually adjust it, and it will cap at, in this case, I'm
still turning that, and it caps at three volts, which is what has been set as the maximum output
amplitude. That's really handy to avoid frying any circuitry. There is another really neat feature
of this supply, in that you can actually set up to nine output voltage and current presets.
So I've actually programmed some in here. So if we go recall, number one, it actually
goes down to one volt, which I've pre-programmed, and 0.1 amps output. And if I go recall two,
enter, it actually recalls what I've previously programmed, two volts and 0.2 amps, and so on.
That's a really handy feature. Now on the back here it's actually got RS-232 and RS-485 inputs,
which is really handy for PC control. I've actually used this one for actually quite some
time, actually more than a year now, so I'm fairly familiar with it. But there are still
modes that I haven't really figured out, and that I don't remember. So operation is really
non-intuitive. That's probably the major gripe I have about this unit, is that you really,
for all but the basic operations, you've really got to read the manual. And even for the basic
stuff, you know, things like it can get into really weird modes that you have no idea about.
And you know, somebody's been playing with this on the bench, and you don't have the manual handy,
and they've set some weird, you know, current limit threshold you don't like. Changing it
can really be quite a chore to figure out. It's just too complicated. I don't like the
user interface. It sucks. Okay, so I've said the user interface sucks. What would I do different
if I was designing a supply like this? Well, for starters, the jog shuttle's really nice.
I would keep that, but I would have separate buttons for voltage and current. Separate
buttons that light up. You don't have to do this press shift all the time. You have to press shift
for everything on this thing. It's crazy. There should be a dedicated output on off button,
dedicated voltage and current button that lights up, so you know exactly what you're setting. You
don't have to decode this small fiddly display here. Well, the settings on the side are quite
small, and they're just really hard to interpret at, you know, just at a glance. The other major
disadvantage of this supply is that you really need more than one. It's only a single output
supply. It'd be much handier if it had a dual tracking, if it was a dual output and had dual
tracking option. That would make it really much better than what it currently is. Now, there are
different models available with different output voltage and current ranges. So this is the 40 volt
5 amp model. There's a 0 to 20 volt unit and like a 0 to 60 volt or something like that.
So there are different models available. I haven't actually tried out the PC functions of this, but
it does look quite comprehensive. It's got data logging capability and all sorts of things. You
can step things, and it's got 99 different programs or something you can program into it.
So if you're after a PC controlled thing, I mean, I'm sure it's fairly good in that respect.
But as a general use lab supply, it's just not that easy to use. I can't really
recommend it as your basic everyday unit, unless you get really intimately familiar with it.
So the verdict on the BK Precision 1697 lab power supply? I give it a tentative thumbs up because
it's quite good value for money, considering that it's PC controlled and it really does have a lot
of functionality and it meets its performance specs. But the user interface, quite frankly,
it sucks and it gets a thumbs down. I hate the user interface. It's awful. But if you can live
with that and you want, you know, a good value for money PC controlled programmable bench supply,
you could do a lot worse than this.
